newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New U.N. moves on W.Sahara await next Baker trip.
newsitem.headline: New U.N. moves on W.Sahara await next Baker trip.

text.p: A forthcoming U.N. report on the disputed territory of Western Sahara is not expected to make any substantive new recommendations pending a further visit to the region by a U.N. envoy, former U.S. Secretary of State James Baker, diplomats said on Friday.
The report, by Secretary-General Kofi Annan, is due to be sent to the Security Council next week.
Baker, who paid an initial visit to the region late April, will probably return some time in June, the diplomats said.
Annan's report was expected to recommend a four-month renewal of the small U.N. force in Western Sahara. Its current six-month mandate expires on May 31.
It was set up to organise and monitor a peace plan calling for a referendum on the future of the territory, originally set for January 1992.

The referendum is to decide whether the former Spanish colony should be incorporated into Morocco, which controls most of the territory, or become independent, as demanded by the Algerian-backed Polisario Front. The referendum has been repeatedly postponed because of disagreements over who should be eligible to vote.
The U.N. force, called the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO), also monitors a ceasefire between Morocco and Polisario which took effect in September 1991.
MINURSO, whose six-month mandate expires on May 31, comprises about 240 military observers plus a small support staff.

Baker was appointed in March as the secretary-general's personal envoy for Western Sahara to recommend whether the peace plan could still be implemented in its present form, whether adjustments acceptable to both sides might be made, or whether other ways of resolving the conflict could be found.
Last month he visited Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and the Polisario base at Tindouf, near Algeria's border with Morocco.
Baker said during the trip he was primarily listening to the parties. He is not expected to make any substantive recommendations to Annan until after his next tour of the region.
